questions.stem: A client presents with bone pain, fatigue, recurrent infections, and elevated serum calcium, with lab work showing abnormal protein levels, and a family member assumes this is just ordinary age-related bone wear and tear. The nurse should instead suspect:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An unrelated endocrine condition needing further workup, which would not fully explain this particular combination of bone, blood, and protein findings","B":"Simple osteoarthritis confirmed without further testing, similar to what the family member is currently assuming about this presentation","C":"Multiple myeloma, a plasma cell cancer, warranting evaluation, rather than the ordinary age-related wear the family member assumed given this specific combination of findings","D":"A normal aging change requiring no further evaluation, contrary to what this constellation of bone pain, infections, and lab abnormalities actually warrants"}}
questions.rationale: Bone pain (from lytic bone lesions), fatigue (from anemia), recurrent infections (from impaired normal antibody production), hypercalcemia (from bone breakdown), and abnormal protein levels (from monoclonal protein production) are classic findings suggestive of multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells, warranting further evaluation, including protein electrophoresis and bone marrow biopsy.
questions.source_name: American Cancer Society — Multiple Myeloma Signs and Symptoms
questions.source_detail: Clinical Presentation Suggestive of Multiple Myeloma

questions.stem: A male infant is diagnosed with hemophilia A, an X-linked recessive bleeding disorder, and a family member assumes this means the baby will have trouble with blood clotting too much rather than too little. The nurse should instead recognize this condition is characterized by:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A Factor VIII deficiency, leading to prolonged bleeding with injury, rather than the excessive clotting the family member is currently assuming this condition causes","B":"Excessive clotting with fairly little associated bleeding risk, similar to what the family member is currently assuming about this diagnosis","C":"A condition with fairly little need for any special precautions, contrary to the precautions this bleeding disorder actually requires","D":"A platelet function disorder largely unrelated to clotting factors, which does not describe the actual clotting-factor mechanism behind this condition"}}
questions.rationale: Hemophilia A results from a deficiency in clotting Factor VIII, leading to impaired blood clotting and prolonged bleeding, particularly notable with injury, surgery, or spontaneous bleeding into joints (hemarthrosis) and muscles. Care includes bleeding precautions, prompt treatment of bleeding episodes, and factor replacement therapy as prescribed.
questions.source_name: National Hemophilia Foundation — Hemophilia A Clinical Overview
questions.source_detail: Pathophysiology and Clinical Features of Hemophilia A

questions.stem: A client with von Willebrand disease, the most common inherited bleeding disorder, asks the nurse whether their bleeding pattern will look just like what they've read about hemophilia. The client would most likely instead present with which type of bleeding pattern?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Only deep muscle and joint bleeding, identical to hemophilia, similar to what this client is currently assuming their own bleeding pattern will look like","B":"No bleeding tendency of any kind associated with this disorder, contrary to the actual bleeding risk this condition carries","C":"Excessive clotting with no associated bleeding risk, which describes the opposite of what this bleeding disorder actually causes","D":"Mucocutaneous bleeding, from impaired platelet adhesion, rather than the joint-and-muscle pattern seen in hemophilia that this client was asking about"}}
questions.rationale: Von Willebrand disease, resulting from a deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor (important for platelet adhesion), typically presents with mucocutaneous bleeding patterns — such as easy bruising, frequent nosebleeds, bleeding gums, and heavy menstrual bleeding — distinct from the deep muscle/joint bleeding pattern more classically associated with hemophilia (a clotting factor deficiency).
questions.source_name: National Hemophilia Foundation — Von Willebrand Disease Clinical Overview
questions.source_detail: Mucocutaneous Bleeding Pattern in Von Willebrand Disease

questions.stem: A client has a platelet count of 25,000/mm³, and a family member encourages the client to keep up their usual daily jog since staying active seems like the healthy thing to do. The nurse should instead implement which precaution given this significant thrombocytopenia?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Encouraging vigorous physical activity with no restriction, similar to what the family member is currently encouraging this client to continue","B":"No specific precautions being needed at this particular platelet count, contrary to the bleeding risk this significantly low count actually poses","C":"Bleeding precautions such as a soft toothbrush and electric razor, rather than continuing vigorous activity as the family member is currently encouraging","D":"Administering aspirin regularly to thin the blood further, which would actually worsen rather than help this client's bleeding risk"}}
questions.rationale: A significantly low platelet count (such as 25,000/mm³, well below the normal range of approximately 150,000-400,000/mm³) places the client at high risk for spontaneous bleeding. Bleeding precautions include using a soft toothbrush, avoiding intramuscular injections and unnecessary invasive procedures when possible, using an electric razor instead of a blade, avoiding activities with high injury risk, and closely monitoring for any signs of bleeding.
questions.source_name: Clinical Hematology References — Thrombocytopenia Bleeding Precautions
questions.source_detail: Nursing Interventions for Significant Thrombocytopenia

questions.stem: A client's fasting blood glucose result is 92 mg/dL. The nurse should recognize this value as:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A dangerously low value requiring immediate treatment","B":"Indicative of prediabetes based on current criteria","C":"Indicative of diabetes based on current criteria","D":"Within the normal fasting range per ADA criteria"}}
questions.rationale: Normal fasting blood glucose is generally below 100 mg/dL, per ADA criteria. A value of 92 mg/dL falls within this normal range, distinct from prediabetes (fasting glucose 100-125 mg/dL) or diabetes (fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL on two occasions).
questions.source_name: American Diabetes Association — Standards of Care, Diagnostic Criteria
questions.source_detail: Normal Fasting Blood Glucose Range

questions.stem: A client's 2-hour postprandial blood glucose comes back significantly elevated, and the client assumes this single reading couldn't really mean much since it was taken right after a big meal. The nurse should recognize this finding as suggestive of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A finding entirely unrelated to diabetes risk, contrary to why this particular postprandial test was actually ordered for this client","B":"Hypoglycemia requiring immediate carbohydrate intake, which is the opposite of what this elevated reading actually indicates","C":"Impaired glucose tolerance, warranting further evaluation, rather than the meaningless post-meal blip the client is currently assuming this represents","D":"Normal glucose metabolism requiring no further testing, contrary to what this significantly elevated result actually warrants"}}
questions.rationale: An elevated 2-hour postprandial blood glucose level suggests impaired glucose tolerance, which may indicate prediabetes or diabetes, warranting further evaluation (such as additional testing, including a formal oral glucose tolerance test or HbA1c) to confirm the diagnosis and guide management.
questions.source_name: American Diabetes Association — Postprandial Glucose Testing Interpretation
questions.source_detail: Significance of Elevated Postprandial Glucose

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing a client for an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), often used to screen for gestational diabetes, and the client assumes this will just be one quick blood draw like a regular lab test. The nurse should explain that this test instead involves:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Measuring glucose at baseline and again after a standardized glucose solution, rather than the single quick draw the client is currently assuming this test involves","B":"A test that measures only urine, not blood, glucose levels, which does not describe how this particular test is actually performed for this client","C":"A single fasting blood draw with no further testing needed, similar to what the client is currently assuming this test will involve","D":"Fairly little fasting or specific preparation required beforehand, contrary to the actual preparation this particular test requires"}}
questions.rationale: An oral glucose tolerance test involves measuring blood glucose at baseline (fasting) and then at specific timed intervals (such as 1 and 2 hours, or additional intervals depending on the specific protocol) after the client ingests a standardized oral glucose solution, assessing how effectively the body processes and clears glucose over time — commonly used to screen for gestational diabetes and sometimes to help diagnose diabetes/prediabetes in non-pregnant individuals.
questions.source_name: American Diabetes Association — Oral Glucose Tolerance Test Protocol
questions.source_detail: Purpose and Procedure of the OGTT

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client with type 1 diabetes how to test for urine ketones during periods of illness or significantly elevated blood glucose, and the client wonders if this test could just replace their usual blood glucose checks to save time. The purpose of this testing is instead to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Measure blood glucose levels directly instead of ketones, which does not describe what this particular urine test is actually designed to detect","B":"Assess kidney function exclusively, not metabolic status, which does not describe the actual purpose of checking for ketones","C":"Identify early signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), rather than replace blood glucose monitoring as the client is currently wondering about","D":"Replace the need for any blood glucose monitoring, similar to what the client is currently wondering whether this test could do"}}
questions.rationale: Urine ketone testing helps identify early signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), since the presence of ketones indicates the body is breaking down fat for energy due to inadequate insulin availability (a state of relative or absolute insulin deficiency), a critical safety check especially during illness or significantly elevated blood glucose in clients with type 1 diabetes, when DKA risk is increased.
questions.source_name: American Diabetes Association — Ketone Testing Guidance for Diabetes Management
questions.source_detail: Purpose of Urine Ketone Testing

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a client's peak expiratory flow (PEF) reading in the context of asthma management, and the reading comes back well below the client's personal best, though the client feels fine at the moment and assumes the number must be a fluke. A PEF reading significantly below personal best, such as less than 50%, generally instead indicates:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A significant asthma exacerbation warranting prompt intervention, rather than the fluke reading the client is currently assuming this represents","B":"Excellent asthma control requiring no further action, contrary to what this particular low reading actually suggests","C":"A normal, expected daily variation requiring no response, contrary to the significance of a reading this far below personal best","D":"A finding unrelated to asthma severity or control, contrary to why this particular measurement is actually tracked for this client"}}
questions.rationale: A peak expiratory flow reading significantly below a client's personal best (such as falling into the "red zone," often defined as less than 50% of personal best in many asthma action plans) generally indicates a significant asthma exacerbation or poor control, warranting prompt intervention according to the client's individualized written asthma action plan, which may include specific medication instructions or seeking urgent medical care.
questions.source_name: GINA (Global Initiative for Asthma) / NAEPP Asthma Action Plan Guidance
questions.source_detail: Interpreting Low Peak Flow Readings

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing HbA1c diagnostic thresholds with a nursing student. Per ADA criteria, an HbA1c of 6.5% or higher on two separate occasions is generally used to diagnose:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Hypoglycemia based on the standard ADA diagnostic criteria","B":"Normal glucose metabolism per current ADA criteria","C":"Diabetes mellitus per current ADA diagnostic criteria","D":"A finding unrelated to glucose control or metabolism"}}
questions.rationale: Per ADA diagnostic criteria, an HbA1c of 6.5% or higher (confirmed on two separate testing occasions, unless there is unequivocal hyperglycemia with classic symptoms) is used to diagnose diabetes mellitus, reflecting average blood glucose control over approximately the preceding 2-3 months. An HbA1c of 5.7%-6.4% generally indicates prediabetes, while below 5.7% is considered normal.
questions.source_name: American Diabetes Association — Standards of Care, HbA1c Diagnostic Criteria
questions.source_detail: HbA1c Thresholds for Diabetes Diagnosis

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to administer a medication and performs the "three checks" of the medication label. These checks generally occur:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Only after the medication has already been given to the client","B":"Checking the medication three times with the same person present","C":"Only once, at a random point during preparation","D":"At removal from storage, preparation, and before administration"}}
questions.rationale: The traditional "three checks" of medication administration involve comparing the medication label to the medication administration record (MAR) at three points: when first removing the medication from storage, when preparing or pouring the dose, and immediately before administering it to the client at the bedside — a safety practice to catch potential errors at multiple points in the process.
questions.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Three Checks of Medication Administration
questions.source_detail: Timing and Purpose of the Three Label Checks

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client with an epidural catheter for pain management, and a newer colleague assumes that once the catheter is placed and working, no further monitoring is really needed beyond checking the pain score. Site care and monitoring should instead include:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Regular site assessment along with monitoring for pain relief and complications, rather than just the pain score alone as the newer colleague is currently assuming is sufficient","B":"Removing the catheter dressing daily regardless of clinical need, which is not the appropriate approach to this particular catheter's dressing care","C":"Allowing the client unrestricted movement with no positioning care, contrary to the positioning attention this type of catheter actually requires","D":"No specific monitoring being needed once the catheter is placed, similar to what the newer colleague is currently assuming about ongoing care"}}
questions.rationale: Nursing care for a client with an epidural catheter includes regular assessment of the insertion site for signs of infection, leakage, or dislodgement, along with monitoring the client's pain relief adequacy and watching for potential complications such as excessive motor block (weakness), hypotension, or respiratory depression (particularly with opioid-containing epidural infusions), per facility protocol.
questions.source_name: ASA / ASPMN — Epidural Analgesia Nursing Care Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Key Elements of Epidural Catheter Site Care and Monitoring

questions.stem: A nurse needs to verify correct nasogastric (NG) tube placement before administering a feeding, and a colleague assumes that once the initial X-ray confirmed placement, nothing further ever needs to be checked again. Along with radiographic confirmation as the gold standard for initial placement, the nurse may also use which supportive method for ongoing verification?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Assuming placement is correct if the client reports no discomfort, which is not a reliable method for this kind of ongoing verification","B":"Measuring external tube length at each use and assessing aspirate, rather than relying solely on the initial X-ray as the colleague is currently assuming is sufficient","C":"No further verification being needed after the initial X-ray, ever, similar to what the colleague is currently assuming about ongoing checks","D":"Listening for bowel sounds in the lower abdomen only, which is not a reliable method for confirming this particular tube's placement"}}
questions.rationale: While X-ray remains the gold standard for confirming initial NG tube placement, ongoing verification for subsequent uses (per many facility protocols) can include measuring and documenting the external tube length at each use (comparing to the length recorded at initial confirmed placement, to help detect migration), along with assessing aspirate characteristics and/or pH when appropriate — auscultation alone (the "whoosh test") is not considered a reliable standalone verification method.
questions.source_name: AACN — Practice Alert, Verification of Feeding Tube Placement
questions.source_detail: Supportive Methods for Ongoing NG Tube Placement Verification

questions.stem: A nurse checks gastric residual volume before administering an intermittent tube feeding and obtains an unusually high volume, and a colleague suggests just doubling the feeding rate afterward to help clear things out faster. The nurse should instead:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Ignoring the finding and proceeding with the full feeding without much regard for this result, contrary to what this elevated residual volume actually calls for","B":"Immediately double the feeding rate to compensate, similar to what the colleague is currently suggesting doing in response to this finding","C":"Automatically discontinuing essentially all future feedings permanently, which overstates the appropriate response to a single elevated residual reading","D":"Follow facility protocol for the residual volume threshold, rather than doubling the rate as the colleague suggested"}}
questions.rationale: When an unusually high gastric residual volume is obtained, the nurse should follow facility-specific protocol (since exact threshold recommendations and practices continue to evolve and vary), which may include holding or delaying the feeding, reassessing the client, and notifying the provider if the finding persists or if the client shows other signs of feeding intolerance (such as nausea, vomiting, or abdominal distention), rather than an automatic, rigid response.
questions.source_name: AACN — Practice Alert, Gastric Residual Volume Management
questions.source_detail: Appropriate Response to Elevated Gastric Residual Volume

questions.stem: A nurse is providing health promotion education about breast health, and a client assumes that once they've had a mammogram, there's really no further reason to also pay attention to their own breast tissue between screenings. The nurse should explain that breast self-awareness/self-exam instead:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Having fairly little value and generally being discouraged, similar to what the client is currently assuming about the value of self-awareness between mammograms","B":"Largely replacing clinical breast exam and mammography, which overstates what self-awareness alone is actually meant to accomplish","C":"Helps build familiarity with normal tissue, alongside rather than instead of clinical screening, addressing the client's assumption that mammograms alone are sufficient","D":"Being relevant just for clients with a family history, contrary to why this practice is actually recommended more broadly"}}
questions.rationale: Breast self-awareness (being familiar with one's own normal breast tissue and promptly reporting any new changes) can support early recognition of potential concerns, but current guidance generally positions this as a complement to, not a replacement for, clinical breast exams and appropriate screening mammography per age/risk-based guidelines, since self-exam alone has not been shown to reduce breast cancer mortality on its own.
questions.source_name: American Cancer Society — Breast Awareness and Screening Guidance
questions.source_detail: Role of Breast Self-Awareness Alongside Clinical Screening

questions.stem: A nurse is providing health promotion education to a young adult male client about testicular self-examination. The nurse should teach the client to be familiar with the normal size, shape, and consistency of the testicles, and to report:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Any new lump, swelling, or change from what is typical for them","B":"Any finding, since all findings require emergency care","C":"Nothing, since testicular self-exam has no value","D":"Only pain, with no attention to lumps or swelling"}}
questions.rationale: Testicular self-examination education encourages young adult males to become familiar with the normal size, shape, and consistency of their testicles, so they can more readily notice and promptly report any new lump, swelling, or other change to a healthcare provider for further evaluation, supporting early detection given that testicular cancer often presents in younger men and is highly treatable when caught early.
questions.source_name: American Cancer Society — Testicular Self-Exam Education
questions.source_detail: Purpose and Teaching Points for Testicular Self-Exam

questions.stem: A nurse is providing sexual health education to a client about reducing the risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Evidence-based recommendations generally include:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Assuming STIs are not a concern if a partner appears healthy","B":"Being relevant only for certain populations, not generally applicable","C":"Consistent barrier use, screening, communication, and vaccination","D":"Avoiding any discussion of sexual health as not a nursing role"}}
questions.rationale: Evidence-based STI prevention education generally includes consistent and correct use of barrier methods (such as condoms), regular STI screening as appropriate to the client's risk factors, open and honest communication with sexual partners, and considering relevant vaccinations (such as the HPV vaccine) where applicable — recognizing that a partner's outward appearance of health does not reliably indicate STI status.
questions.source_name: CDC — STI Prevention Recommendations
questions.source_detail: Evidence-Based Strategies for STI Risk Reduction

questions.stem: A client recently diagnosed with a serious illness insists there must be a mistake and continues making plans as though nothing is wrong. The nurse should recognize this as a possible example of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Sublimation, redirecting an urge into an acceptable outlet","B":"Regression, reverting to an earlier developmental stage","C":"Denial, refusing to acknowledge a painful or threatening reality","D":"A permanent, unchangeable psychological state with no resolution"}}
questions.rationale: Denial is a defense mechanism in which a person refuses to acknowledge a painful, threatening, or overwhelming reality, often serving as an initial, temporary buffer against emotional shock following difficult news such as a serious diagnosis. While it can be a normal part of an initial coping process, the nurse should continue to monitor whether it evolves into a barrier to necessary care engagement over time.
questions.source_name: Psychiatric-Mental Health Nursing Foundations — Denial as a Defense Mechanism
questions.source_detail: Recognition and Understanding of Denial in Response to Difficult News

questions.stem: A nurse incorporates attention to a client's spiritual needs and beliefs as part of holistic nursing care. This practice reflects the understanding that:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Spiritual assessment having no place in nursing practice","B":"Spirituality being an important source of meaning and coping","C":"Spirituality being irrelevant to outcomes and not addressed","D":"Spiritual care being provided only if beliefs are shared"}}
questions.rationale: Attending to a client's spiritual needs and beliefs (which may or may not be tied to organized religion) reflects a holistic, patient-centered approach to nursing care, recognizing that spirituality can be an important source of meaning, coping, and support for many clients, particularly during illness, crisis, or end of life — nurses provide spiritual support respectfully regardless of whether they share the client's specific beliefs, and involve chaplaincy or other spiritual care resources as appropriate.
questions.source_name: ANA — Holistic Nursing: Scope and Standards of Practice, Spiritual Care
questions.source_detail: Role of Spirituality in Holistic Nursing Care

questions.stem: A nurse uses a structured cultural assessment tool or framework during an admission interview to better understand a client's cultural background and health-related beliefs, and a colleague suggests it would be quicker to just guess based on the client's apparent ethnicity instead. This practice instead supports:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A systematic, individualized approach to cultural understanding, rather than the assumption-based shortcut the colleague is currently suggesting","B":"Replacing the need for any further individualized communication, which is not the actual purpose of using this kind of structured tool","C":"A practice with no established value in nursing care, contrary to why this structured tool is actually used during admission","D":"Making assumptions about the client based on apparent ethnicity, similar to the shortcut the colleague is currently suggesting instead of using the tool"}}
questions.rationale: Using a structured cultural assessment tool or framework supports a systematic, individualized approach to understanding a specific client's cultural values, beliefs, and preferences relevant to their care, helping avoid reliance on broad generalizations or assumptions based on apparent ethnicity or background, and instead centering the client's own expressed identity and needs.
questions.source_name: Transcultural Nursing Society — Cultural Assessment Tools and Frameworks
questions.source_detail: Value of Structured, Individualized Cultural Assessment

questions.stem: A client with supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is treated with IV adenosine, and the client's spouse worries this medication might cause lasting discomfort afterward. The nurse should teach the client to expect which brief sensation immediately after administration?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Brief chest pressure, flushing, or a sense of impending doom, resolving within seconds, rather than the lasting discomfort the spouse is currently worried about","B":"Severe, lasting pain requiring opioid treatment, which overstates the brief, self-resolving nature of this medication's typical effect","C":"Prolonged sedation lasting several hours afterward, which does not describe how this particular medication actually affects the client","D":"No sensation at all following administration, contrary to the brief sensation clients commonly do experience with this medication"}}
questions.rationale: Adenosine has an extremely short half-life (seconds), and clients commonly experience a brief, unsettling sensation of chest pressure, flushing, or impending doom, along with a very brief pause in the cardiac rhythm (as adenosine transiently blocks AV node conduction to terminate the SVT), which typically resolves within seconds given the drug's rapid clearance.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Adenosine
questions.source_detail: Expected Transient Effects of Adenosine Administration

questions.stem: A client on long-term procainamide therapy for an arrhythmia develops joint pain, rash, and a positive antinuclear antibody test, and the provider initially assumes this must be an unrelated new autoimmune condition unconnected to the medication. The nurse should instead recognize this as a possible sign of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An unrelated autoimmune condition with no medication connection, similar to what the provider is currently assuming about this presentation","B":"Improved therapeutic response requiring a dose increase, which misreads these findings as a positive rather than concerning sign","C":"A normal, expected medication effect requiring no action, contrary to what this particular combination of findings actually calls for","D":"Drug-induced lupus-like syndrome, a recognized adverse effect of this medication, rather than the unrelated new condition the provider initially assumed"}}
questions.rationale: Long-term procainamide therapy carries a well-recognized risk of drug-induced lupus-like syndrome, presenting with symptoms such as joint pain, rash, and positive antinuclear antibodies, generally reversible upon discontinuation of the medication, requiring provider notification and further evaluation.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Procainamide
questions.source_detail: Warnings: Drug-Induced Lupus-Like Syndrome

questions.stem: A nurse anticipates administering oxytocin to a client immediately after delivery of the placenta, and a family member assumes this medication is being given to help induce further labor contractions. The purpose of this medication in this particular context is instead to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Induce labor contractions in the antepartum period, which does not describe why oxytocin is actually being given at this particular postpartum moment","B":"Promote uterine contraction to prevent postpartum hemorrhage, rather than induce labor as the family member is currently assuming","C":"Relieve postpartum pain at the delivery site, which is not the actual purpose of oxytocin in this particular clinical context","D":"Prevent the onset of postpartum depression, which is not an effect or purpose associated with this particular medication"}}
questions.rationale: After delivery of the placenta, oxytocin is commonly administered to promote firm uterine contraction (uterine tone), which helps compress the blood vessels at the placental implantation site, reducing the risk of postpartum hemorrhage — a distinct indication from its use in labor induction/augmentation.
questions.source_name: ACOG — Postpartum Hemorrhage Prevention Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Oxytocin Use for Postpartum Hemorrhage Prevention

questions.stem: A provider considers methylergonovine for a postpartum client with significant bleeding, and a nursing student assumes this medication would be safe to give to essentially any postpartum client experiencing heavy bleeding. The nurse should recognize this medication is instead contraindicated in clients with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A history of a prior cesarean birth, which is not an actual contraindication for this particular medication","B":"A vasoconstrictive drug best avoided in someone with high blood pressure or preeclampsia, given the added strain that could cause","C":"No specific contraindications existing for this medication, similar to what the nursing student is currently assuming","D":"A history of gestational diabetes in this same pregnancy, which is not an actual reason to avoid this particular medication"}}
questions.rationale: Methylergonovine causes significant vasoconstriction as part of its uterotonic effect, and is contraindicated in clients with hypertension or preeclampsia, since it can further and dangerously elevate blood pressure. The nurse should verify blood pressure history before this medication is administered and monitor closely if given.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Methylergonovine
questions.source_detail: Contraindication in Hypertension and Preeclampsia

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client receiving misoprostol for labor induction/cervical ripening, and a colleague assumes the main thing to watch for is simply a drop in the client's blood pressure. The nurse should instead monitor closely for which potential complication associated with this medication?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Uterine tachysystole, which can affect fetal oxygenation, rather than simply the blood pressure drop the colleague is currently assuming is the main concern","B":"Hypotension exclusively, without much other concern, similar to what the colleague is currently assuming is the primary thing to watch for","C":"No specific monitoring being needed with this medication, contrary to the close monitoring this particular medication actually requires","D":"Improved fetal heart rate without much other consideration, which does not describe the actual risk this medication carries for the fetus"}}
questions.rationale: Misoprostol, used for cervical ripening/labor induction, carries a risk of uterine tachysystole (excessive contraction frequency), which can reduce placental blood flow and affect fetal oxygenation. Close monitoring of uterine contraction pattern and fetal heart rate is essential during administration, with the medication discontinued/withheld if tachysystole or fetal distress occurs.
questions.source_name: ACOG — Misoprostol Use for Labor Induction, Monitoring Requirements
questions.source_detail: Uterine Tachysystole Risk with Misoprostol

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for an Rh-negative pregnant client, and the client assumes Rho(D) immune globulin (RhoGAM) is only ever given right after delivery if needed, with nothing required earlier in the pregnancy. RhoGAM is typically instead administered at approximately which point during pregnancy, in addition to after delivery if the newborn is Rh-positive?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Only after delivery, with no antepartum dosing at all, similar to what the client is currently assuming about the timing of this medication","B":"Only in the first trimester, with no further dosing, which does not describe the actual typical timing of this medication during pregnancy","C":"Never during pregnancy, only in the postpartum period, similar to the client's current assumption about when this medication is given","D":"Around 28 weeks gestation, plus postpartum if indicated, rather than only after delivery as the client is currently assuming"}}
questions.rationale: Rho(D) immune globulin is typically administered to Rh-negative pregnant clients at approximately 28 weeks gestation as a standard antepartum dose, in addition to a postpartum dose if the newborn is confirmed Rh-positive, and after any event with potential fetal-maternal blood exposure (such as amniocentesis, trauma, or vaginal bleeding), to help prevent maternal Rh sensitization.
questions.source_name: ACOG — Rh(D) Immune Globulin Administration Timing
questions.source_detail: Standard Antepartum and Postpartum RhoGAM Dosing Schedule

questions.stem: A nurse is administering IV promethazine and understands this medication carries a significant risk of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"No notable administration-related risks with this route","B":"Severe tissue injury if extravasation or intra-arterial injection occurs","C":"Guaranteed safety regardless of administration technique","D":"Improved venous health with repeated IV push administration"}}
questions.rationale: IV promethazine carries a well-documented risk of severe tissue injury, including necrosis and gangrene, particularly if the medication extravasates into surrounding tissue or is inadvertently administered intra-arterially. Given this significant risk, FDA warnings and safety guidance recommend extreme caution with IV administration, and many institutions have shifted toward preferring alternative routes or highly diluted, slow administration through a well-functioning, larger vein when IV use is necessary.
questions.source_name: FDA — Boxed Warning for Promethazine, Tissue Injury Risk
questions.source_detail: Severe Tissue Damage Risk with IV Administration

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a promethazine order for a very young child, and the ordering provider seems unaware of any particular age-related concern with this medication in young children. The nurse should recognize that promethazine carries an FDA warning regarding:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A recommendation for routine use in all pediatric age groups without exception, which does not describe the actual FDA warning associated with this medication","B":"There being no relevant pediatric warnings of any kind for this particular drug, similar to what the ordering provider currently seems to assume","C":"An improved safety profile specifically in very young children under two, which is the opposite of the actual FDA warning associated with this medication","D":"Contraindication under age 2 due to fatal respiratory depression risk, contrary to what the ordering provider currently seems to assume about this medication's safety in a very young child"}}
questions.rationale: FDA labeling for promethazine includes a contraindication for use in children younger than 2 years due to the risk of severe, potentially fatal respiratory depression, with caution advised even in older pediatric clients. The nurse should verify the child's age and question any order for promethazine in a child under 2 before administration.
questions.source_name: FDA — Boxed Warning for Promethazine, Pediatric Respiratory Depression Risk
questions.source_detail: Contraindication in Children Younger Than 2 Years

questions.stem: A nurse caring for a client receiving IV magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia is reminded by a colleague to check deep tendon reflexes regularly, though the colleague doesn't mention anything else to watch given the risk of magnesium toxicity. The nurse should also monitor which vital sign closely?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Respiratory rate, since depression can progress to arrest, an important addition to the deep tendon reflex checks the colleague already mentioned","B":"Core body temperature alone, without factoring in the client's breathing status or pattern at all during this assessment","C":"How the client's skin appears overall, rather than tracking their actual breathing pattern closely during this critical period","D":"Finger-stick glucose results checked periodically throughout the shift, leaving out any attention to the client's own breathing"}}
questions.rationale: In addition to monitoring deep tendon reflexes (loss of which is an early sign of toxicity), the nurse must closely monitor respiratory rate during magnesium sulfate infusion, since respiratory depression is a serious sign of progressing magnesium toxicity that, if untreated, can progress to respiratory arrest and cardiac arrest, requiring immediate intervention including stopping the infusion and administering calcium gluconate.
questions.source_name: Obstetric Magnesium Sulfate Safety Guidelines — Respiratory Monitoring
questions.source_detail: Respiratory Rate Monitoring for Magnesium Toxicity

questions.stem: A client receiving prolonged terbutaline therapy for preterm labor tocolysis should be monitored closely for which serious maternal complication?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"No serious complications are associated with this medication","B":"Improved renal function with no associated risk","C":"Pulmonary edema, particularly with concurrent IV fluid use","D":"Hypoglycemia exclusively, with no other concern"}}
questions.rationale: Prolonged beta-agonist tocolytic therapy (such as terbutaline) carries a risk of maternal pulmonary edema, particularly when combined with significant IV fluid administration (sometimes used concurrently for other obstetric reasons). Close monitoring of respiratory status, fluid balance, and maternal vital signs is important during prolonged tocolytic therapy.
questions.source_name: FDA Drug Safety Communication — Terbutaline, Prolonged Use Risks
questions.source_detail: Pulmonary Edema Risk with Prolonged Tocolytic Therapy

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a medication order that uses the abbreviation "U" for units. The nurse should recognize this as:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An acceptable, standard abbreviation with no safety concern","B":"A newly recommended abbreviation for improved clarity","C":"An error-prone abbreviation on the 'Do Not Use' list","D":"An abbreviation with no relevance to patient safety"}}
questions.rationale: The abbreviation "U" for units is on The Joint Commission's official "Do Not Use" list of error-prone abbreviations, since it can be mistaken for a zero (leading to a tenfold overdose) or the number 4, among other misreadings. The word "units" should be spelled out completely to prevent this type of serious medication error.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — Official "Do Not Use" List of Abbreviations
questions.source_detail: "U" for Units as a Prohibited Error-Prone Abbreviation

questions.stem: A nurse notices a medication label uses "tall man lettering," such as "hydrOXYzine" and "hydrALAZINE." The purpose of this labeling convention is to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Visually emphasizing distinguishing letters in similar drug names","B":"Showing the medication is a scheduled controlled substance","C":"Making the label more difficult for staff to read","D":"Indicating the medication has passed its expiration date"}}
questions.rationale: Tall man lettering is a labeling convention that visually emphasizes (through capitalization) the distinguishing letters between look-alike, sound-alike (LASA) medication names, such as hydrOXYzine and hydrALAZINE, helping draw attention to the key differences and reduce the risk of selecting or administering the wrong medication due to name confusion.
questions.source_name: ISMP — Tall Man Lettering for Look-Alike, Sound-Alike Drug Names
questions.source_detail: Purpose of Tall Man Lettering Convention

questions.stem: A hospital policy restricts verbal medication orders to situations of clinical urgency, discouraging their routine use for non-urgent situations, and a provider questions why this restriction exists when verbal orders seem quicker and just as reliable as written ones. This policy reflects the understanding that verbal orders are instead:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Having fairly little relationship to patient safety, contrary to why this restriction exists in the first place","B":"A method carrying more risk for mishearing or miscommunication, which is why it's saved for genuinely urgent moments","C":"A policy with no supporting clinical evidence base, contrary to the actual evidence behind why this restriction exists","D":"Being generally safer than written orders, which is essentially the opposite of the actual reasoning behind this particular policy"}}
questions.rationale: Verbal orders carry a higher inherent risk of miscommunication or error (due to potential mishearing, accents, background noise, or other factors) compared to written or electronic orders, so best practice and many facility policies restrict their use to situations of genuine clinical urgency, where the time-sensitivity justifies this increased risk, with read-back verification required when they are used.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — Verbal Order Policy and Safety Rationale
questions.source_detail: Rationale for Restricting Verbal Order Use

questions.stem: A nurse administers a medication per a pre-approved standing order protocol, without needing to contact the provider for that specific instance, and a student assumes standing orders must only exist in outpatient clinics rather than hospital settings. Standing orders are instead:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Used just in outpatient settings, never in hospitals, similar to what the student is currently assuming about where these protocols are actually used","B":"Pre-approved protocols letting a nurse begin certain care without first calling for a fresh order each time","C":"Rarely permitted in any healthcare setting or context, contrary to the fact that this nurse is actually using one right now in this scenario","D":"Identical to verbal orders with fairly little meaningful distinction, which does not accurately describe how these two types of orders actually differ"}}
questions.rationale: Standing orders are pre-established, provider-approved protocols (developed and periodically reviewed by the medical and nursing staff) that allow nurses to initiate specific interventions under clearly defined clinical circumstances, without requiring a new individual order for each instance — streamlining care for common, predictable clinical situations while maintaining appropriate oversight and defined parameters.
questions.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Standing Orders and Protocols
questions.source_detail: Purpose and Use of Standing Order Protocols

questions.stem: A nurse receives a telephone order from a provider for a new medication, and a colleague assumes telephone orders are handled with exactly the same considerations as any in-person verbal order with nothing extra to think about. In addition to read-back verification, the nurse should instead be aware that telephone orders are:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Identical to in-person verbal orders with no distinction, similar to what the colleague is currently assuming about this type of order","B":"Requiring no documentation once read-back is completed, contrary to the documentation this type of order still actually requires","C":"Permitted for all situations with no additional considerations, contrary to the added restrictions this type of order actually carries","D":"Facing additional restrictions given the added communication risk, rather than being treated identically to in-person orders as the colleague assumed"}}
questions.rationale: Beyond general read-back verification requirements, some facilities and regulatory frameworks place additional restrictions on telephone orders, such as limiting their use for certain high-risk medication categories or requiring the ordering provider to co-sign the order within a specific timeframe, reflecting the recognition that telephone communication (without visual/nonverbal cues) carries added risk of miscommunication compared to in-person verbal orders.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission / Facility Policy — Telephone Order Requirements
questions.source_detail: Additional Considerations for Telephone Order Safety

questions.stem: A hospital implements "smart pump" IV infusion technology with built-in dose error-reduction software, and a nurse wonders whether this technology now means double-checking pump settings manually is no longer really necessary. This technology helps prevent errors by:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Having fairly little impact on IV medication safety, contrary to why hospitals actually implement this particular technology today","B":"Alerting staff when a dose falls outside pre-established safe limits, rather than eliminating the need for the nurse's own verification as the nurse is currently wondering about","C":"Automatically correcting errors largely without any nurse awareness, which overstates what this technology is actually designed to do on its own","D":"Eliminating the need for any nursing verification of pump settings at all, similar to what the nurse is currently wondering whether this technology allows"}}
questions.rationale: Smart pump technology includes built-in dose error-reduction software with a drug library containing pre-established safe dosing limits for various medications. When a nurse programs an infusion rate or dose that falls outside these established safe limits, the pump alerts the nurse, prompting review and correction before the infusion proceeds — though the nurse must still verify pump settings, since the technology is a safeguard, not a replacement for clinical verification.
questions.source_name: ISMP — Smart Pump Technology Safety Benefits
questions.source_detail: Function of Dose Error-Reduction Software in Smart Pumps

questions.stem: A nurse is programming an IV infusion pump for a high-alert medication, such as an insulin or heparin infusion, and a colleague suggests skipping the second check since the nurse has programmed this exact rate many times before. Best practice instead includes:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Verification only for oral medications, not IV infusions, which does not describe the actual scope of double-check requirements for this kind of high-alert drug","B":"An independent double-check of pump programming by a second nurse, rather than skipping it based on prior experience as the colleague suggested","C":"Skipping verification if the nurse feels confident enough, similar to what the colleague is currently suggesting given the nurse's familiarity with this rate","D":"Programming the pump independently with no second-nurse check, similar to what the colleague is currently suggesting for this particular infusion"}}
questions.rationale: For high-alert medications administered via IV infusion (such as insulin or heparin), best practice includes an independent double-check of the pump programming (verifying the rate, concentration, and total dose) by a second qualified nurse before the infusion begins, in addition to leveraging smart pump technology safeguards where available — a critical safety step given the significant potential for harm if a programming error occurs with these medications.
questions.source_name: ISMP — High-Alert Medication Independent Double-Check Recommendations
questions.source_detail: Double-Check Requirement for High-Alert IV Infusions

questions.stem: A nurse encounters a barcode medication administration (BCMA) system alert indicating a potential mismatch, and considers overriding the alert since these alerts have seemed like false alarms most of the time lately. The nurse should instead understand that overrides should be:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Used cautiously and only after carefully verifying the situation, rather than routinely dismissed based on a recent pattern of false alarms as the nurse is currently considering","B":"Used routinely without further thought, since alerts often false-positive, similar to what the nurse is currently considering doing based on recent experience","C":"Never permitted, even when clinically appropriate to do so after careful verification, which overstates the actual restriction on this kind of override","D":"Treated as having no clinical significance to ignore, similar to what the nurse is currently leaning toward given the recent pattern of alerts"}}
questions.rationale: While BCMA override functionality may sometimes be necessary for legitimate clinical reasons, it should be used cautiously, only after the nurse carefully verifies the situation and confirms it is genuinely safe to proceed, since research has shown that frequent, routine, or careless overriding of BCMA alerts undermines the safety value of the system and has been associated with medication errors reaching the patient.
questions.source_name: ISMP — Barcode Medication Administration Override Risks
questions.source_detail: Appropriate, Cautious Use of BCMA Override Functionality

questions.stem: A hospital transitions from conducting shift-to-shift report exclusively at the nurses' station to conducting bedside shift report, with the client present when possible, though a veteran nurse worries this change will actually make the client feel like just an object being discussed. Benefits of this newer approach instead include:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Reduced patient involvement in their own care overall, contrary to the actual goal and effect of this newer bedside reporting approach","B":"Decreased accuracy of information transfer between shifts, contrary to the improved accuracy this approach is actually intended to support","C":"No meaningful difference from station-based reporting, contrary to the specific benefits this bedside approach is actually designed to provide","D":"Increased engagement, since both nurses assess the client together with the client present, rather than the objectifying experience the veteran nurse is worried about"}}
questions.rationale: Bedside shift report, with the client present when appropriate and desired, is associated with increased patient engagement (allowing the client to participate in and help verify shared information) and improved safety, since both the outgoing and incoming nurses can visually assess the client together at the start of the shift, potentially catching issues (such as a change in a dressing or IV site) that might otherwise be missed.
questions.source_name: AHRQ — Bedside Shift Report Implementation Guide
questions.source_detail: Benefits of Bedside vs. Station-Based Shift Report

questions.stem: A nursing unit implements a structured hourly rounding protocol, in which nurses check on each client at regular intervals to proactively address common needs, and a skeptical staff member assumes this will just add busywork without actually changing outcomes like falls. The purpose of this practice is instead to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Replacing the need for responding to call lights largely, which is not the actual purpose or effect of this particular rounding protocol","B":"Applying just to clients at high fall risk, with fairly little other benefit, which understates how broadly this protocol is actually intended to help","C":"Increase nursing workload with no measurable patient benefit, similar to what the skeptical staff member is currently assuming about this protocol","D":"Proactively address needs, reducing falls and improving satisfaction, rather than simply adding busywork as the skeptical staff member assumed"}}
questions.rationale: Structured hourly rounding protocols, in which nurses proactively check on clients at regular intervals to address common needs (pain, positioning, toileting, and ensuring personal items are within reach), have been associated in research with reduced fall rates, decreased call light use, and improved patient satisfaction, reflecting a proactive rather than purely reactive approach to care.
questions.source_name: Studer Group / AHRQ — Hourly Rounding Evidence and Implementation
questions.source_detail: Purpose and Benefits of Structured Hourly Rounding

questions.stem: A nurse manager conducts regular "leader rounding," visiting client rooms and staff work areas to check in directly. The purpose of this practice includes:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Replacing the need for staff to communicate through any other channel","B":"Gaining firsthand insight into patient experience and staff needs","C":"Micromanaging staff with no other meaningful purpose","D":"Applying only to underperforming units, not others"}}
questions.rationale: Leader rounding — in which nursing leaders regularly visit client rooms and staff work areas — is intended to provide firsthand insight into patient experience and staff needs or concerns, demonstrate visible, accessible leadership presence, and identify opportunities for improvement, recognition, or timely issue resolution, supporting both patient satisfaction and staff engagement.
questions.source_name: Studer Group — Leader Rounding Best Practices
questions.source_detail: Purpose and Value of Leader Rounding

questions.stem: A hospital fosters a "blameless" or "just culture" reporting environment, in which staff are encouraged to report errors and near misses without fear of automatic punitive action, though a new hire assumes this just means nobody is ever held accountable for anything. This approach is instead important because it:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Has no impact on the quantity or quality of reporting, contrary to why this kind of reporting culture is actually fostered","B":"Encourages more complete, honest reporting of safety events, rather than eliminating all accountability as the new hire is currently assuming","C":"Eliminates all accountability for staff actions entirely, similar to what the new hire is currently assuming this approach actually means","D":"Applies only to reckless behavior, with no distinction from ordinary human error, which misstates how this approach actually differentiates between the two"}}
questions.rationale: A blameless or "just culture" reporting environment, which distinguishes between simple human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior (with appropriate, proportionate responses to each, per just culture principles), encourages more complete and honest reporting of safety events. This provides the organization with more accurate data to identify and address systemic issues, ultimately supporting more effective patient safety improvement than a purely punitive culture, which tends to suppress reporting.
questions.source_name: IHI — Just Culture and Blameless Reporting Principles
questions.source_detail: Impact of Reporting Culture on Safety Event Disclosure

questions.stem: A nurse manager fosters an environment in which team members feel comfortable speaking up about concerns, asking questions, or admitting mistakes without fear of embarrassment or retribution, and a colleague from another unit assumes this kind of environment is really just a soft, feel-good idea with no real impact on performance. This team characteristic is instead known as:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A concept with fairly little relevance to healthcare teams, similar to what the colleague from the other unit is currently assuming about this idea","B":"A characteristic relevant just to non-clinical teams, which understates how this concept actually applies to clinical teams like this one","C":"Psychological safety, improving team performance and learning, rather than being a purely feel-good idea with no real impact as the colleague assumed","D":"Excessive permissiveness with no accountability structure, similar to what the colleague from the other unit is currently assuming this fosters"}}
questions.rationale: Psychological safety — a team environment in which members feel comfortable speaking up about concerns, asking questions, admitting mistakes, or offering ideas without fear of embarrassment or retribution — is associated in research with improved team performance, learning, innovation, and patient safety outcomes, an increasingly recognized and valued characteristic of high-functioning healthcare teams.
questions.source_name: Harvard Business School / AHRQ — Psychological Safety in Healthcare Teams
questions.source_detail: Psychological Safety and Its Impact on Team Performance

questions.stem: A hospital conducts regular nurse engagement surveys, gathering staff feedback on job satisfaction, workplace culture, and professional fulfillment. This data is used to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Identifying trends to guide strategies improving retention and care","B":"Punishing units that receive lower engagement scores","C":"Replacing the need for any other quality improvement initiatives","D":"Having no practical application within the organization"}}
questions.rationale: Nurse engagement survey data is used to identify trends and specific areas of concern within the work environment, guiding targeted organizational strategies to improve staff satisfaction, retention, and professional fulfillment — recognizing the well-established connection between staff engagement/well-being and patient care quality, rather than serving a punitive purpose.
questions.source_name: Press Ganey / AONL — Nurse Engagement Survey Purpose and Application
questions.source_detail: Using Engagement Data to Drive Organizational Improvement

questions.stem: During bedside shift report, both the outgoing and incoming nurses jointly verify key safety elements, such as IV site condition and drain/tube patency, though a busy nurse suggests skipping this joint check to save a few minutes since the chart already documents everything. This joint verification practice specifically instead helps:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Catch potential discrepancies at the point of transition, rather than relying solely on chart documentation as the busy nurse is currently suggesting is sufficient","B":"Slow down the shift change process with no safety benefit, similar to what the busy nurse is currently implying by wanting to skip this step","C":"Apply only to critical care settings, not other units, which understates how broadly this joint verification practice is actually used","D":"Replace the need for individual assessment throughout the shift, which is not the actual purpose of this joint verification step"}}
questions.rationale: Joint verification of key safety elements (such as IV site condition, drain/tube patency, and skin integrity) during bedside shift report by both the outgoing and incoming nurses specifically helps catch potential discrepancies or issues at the point of transition — a recognized high-risk time for errors or missed information — supporting continuity and safety of care as responsibility transfers between nurses.
questions.source_name: AHRQ — Bedside Shift Report Safety Verification Elements
questions.source_detail: Value of Joint Safety Verification During Handoff

questions.stem: A nurse notices subtle but concerning changes in a client's condition that do not yet meet criteria for a full code but raise concern for clinical deterioration, and activates the hospital's Rapid Response Team, though a colleague questions why this was called before things got more serious. This system is instead designed to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Being used just once a client has already fully coded, contrary to why the nurse activated this system based on subtle, early changes instead","B":"Applying just in intensive care settings, not elsewhere, which understates where this kind of rapid response system is actually meant to be used","C":"Replace the primary nurse's ongoing responsibility for the client, which is not the actual purpose of activating this particular team","D":"Bring critical care expertise to the bedside early, rather than waiting for a full code as the colleague's question is currently suggesting would have been more appropriate"}}
questions.rationale: Rapid Response Teams are designed to bring critical care expertise to the bedside early, in response to subtle but concerning signs of clinical deterioration (before a full cardiac or respiratory arrest occurs), with the goal of intervening early enough to potentially prevent progression to a more severe event, and any staff member (including nurses on general medical-surgical units) should feel empowered to activate the team when concerned.
questions.source_name: IHI — Rapid Response Team Implementation and Purpose
questions.source_detail: Early Activation to Prevent Clinical Deterioration

questions.stem: An infant presents with wheezing, tachypnea, nasal congestion, and increased work of breathing following a preceding upper respiratory illness, and a family member assumes this is probably just new teething discomfort making the baby breathe a bit differently. The nurse should instead suspect:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Bronchiolitis, commonly caused by RSV in young children, rather than the teething discomfort the family member is currently assuming explains this presentation","B":"Simple teething discomfort with no respiratory involvement, similar to what the family member is currently assuming about this infant's symptoms","C":"A normal cold requiring no further clinical evaluation, contrary to what this particular combination of respiratory findings actually warrants","D":"An unrelated cardiac condition requiring cardiology referral, which would not explain the preceding respiratory illness and current findings together"}}
questions.rationale: Wheezing, tachypnea, nasal congestion, and increased work of breathing following a preceding viral upper respiratory illness are classic findings of bronchiolitis, most commonly caused by RSV, primarily affecting infants and young children under 2 years old, and requiring supportive care with close monitoring of respiratory status, particularly in higher-risk infants.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Bronchiolitis Clinical Practice Guideline
questions.source_detail: Clinical Presentation of RSV Bronchiolitis

questions.stem: A child presents with severe paroxysmal coughing fits followed by a high-pitched "whoop" sound on inspiration, along with post-tussive vomiting, and a parent assumes this must just be a bad cold that happens to make the child cough especially hard. The nurse should instead suspect:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Simple allergies with no infectious or contagious component, contrary to the actual contagious, infectious nature of what this presentation suggests","B":"A normal cold requiring no further clinical evaluation, similar to what the parent is currently assuming given how hard the child is coughing","C":"Pertussis, a highly contagious bacterial respiratory infection, rather than the especially bad cold the parent is currently assuming this represents","D":"An unrelated cardiac condition requiring cardiology referral, which would not explain this particular cough pattern and whooping sound"}}
questions.rationale: Severe paroxysmal coughing fits followed by a characteristic high-pitched "whoop" on inspiration, along with post-tussive vomiting, are classic findings of pertussis (whooping cough), a highly contagious bacterial infection preventable by vaccination, requiring prompt recognition, appropriate precautions, and treatment.
questions.source_name: CDC — Pertussis Clinical Features and Diagnosis
questions.source_detail: Classic Presentation of Whooping Cough

questions.stem: A child presents with high fever, cough, conjunctivitis, coryza, and a characteristic rash that began on the face and spread downward, along with small white spots inside the mouth known as Koplik spots, and a parent assumes this is just a typical viral rash that doesn't need any special precautions. The nurse should instead suspect:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A simple allergic reaction with no infectious component, contrary to the highly contagious infectious process this particular symptom combination suggests","B":"An unrelated bacterial skin infection needing topical care, which would not explain the fever, conjunctivitis, and Koplik spots together","C":"Measles, a highly contagious infection requiring airborne precautions, rather than the typical viral rash the parent is currently assuming needs no special precautions","D":"A normal viral illness requiring no specific precautions, similar to what the parent is currently assuming about this child's presentation"}}
questions.rationale: High fever, cough, conjunctivitis, coryza, Koplik spots (small white spots inside the mouth, considered pathognomonic), and a characteristic rash spreading from the face downward are classic findings of measles, a highly contagious viral infection requiring airborne precautions and prompt public health notification, given its significant complication risk and outbreak potential, especially in under-vaccinated populations.
questions.source_name: CDC — Measles Clinical Features and Infection Control
questions.source_detail: Classic Presentation and Precaution Requirements for Measles

questions.stem: A client presents with fever and painful, unilateral or bilateral swelling of the parotid salivary glands, and a family member assumes this must be an allergic reaction to something the client recently ate. The nurse should instead suspect:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Mumps, a viral infection preventable by vaccination, rather than the allergic reaction the family member is currently assuming caused this presentation","B":"A simple allergic reaction affecting the salivary glands, similar to what the family member is currently assuming about this client's swelling and fever","C":"An unrelated thyroid condition requiring endocrine referral, which would not explain this particular pattern of parotid swelling and fever","D":"A normal dental issue requiring no further evaluation, contrary to what this fever and salivary gland swelling combination actually warrants"}}
questions.rationale: Fever with painful, unilateral or bilateral swelling of the parotid glands (parotitis) is the classic presentation of mumps, a viral infection preventable by the MMR vaccine, which can be associated with complications such as orchitis, meningitis, or pancreatitis in some cases, requiring supportive care and appropriate droplet precautions.
questions.source_name: CDC — Mumps Clinical Features and Complications
questions.source_detail: Classic Parotitis Presentation of Mumps
